headline: Run 5's five findings are fixed. With D119 the mask now covers every long number, the amounts survive, and no code or raw-text key reaches the outbox. One Major remains: a TAC whose digits carry keycap or variation marks, an invisible joiner, or bullet or colon grouping is kept and stored readable. Both lines of defence miss it.

findings.title: A TAC with the strongest keyword is stored readable, unmasked and unmarked, when its digits carry combining or invisible marks, or are grouped by a bullet or colons
findings.detail:
D119 says the mask reads digits "as the filter reads them (any Unicode digit, across spaces, dashes, dots, brackets and invisible characters)", so that "a code never reaches storage". Some shapes get past both lines of defence. The filter's `CANDIDATE` needs `\p{N}+` runs joined only by a space or hyphen. NFKC removes none of U+FE0F, U+20E3, U+FE0E or U+034F. The mask's `kind()` classes these as `OTHER`, which ends a run. So `Your TAC is 4️⃣8️⃣2️⃣9️⃣1️⃣3️⃣.` (keycap emoji digits), `Your TAC is 4︎8︎2︎9︎1︎3.` (variation selector), `Your TAC is 482\u034F913.` (combining grapheme joiner, invisible), `Your TAC is 482•913.` and `Your TAC is 48:29:13.` are all **kept**, with the code readable on screen and `maybe_otp = 0`. Nothing was masked, so nothing is marked.

In fairness, none of these is a shape a Malaysian bank is known to use. But the gate also runs on any app chosen through *More*. The CLAUDE.md rule is about the OTP itself ("discarded … before anything is stored"), and D116/D119 exist so that a shape nobody predicted can't leak. The variation selector and CGJ fall squarely under D119's "invisible characters".

Suggested fix: in both `OtpFilter.sentences` and `OtpMask.kind`, treat every `\p{M}` (combining and enclosing marks) and every default-ignorable code point (U+034F, U+FE00–FE0F, U+180B–180F, U+2060–206F, U+E0000 block) as invisible. Consider treating `•` (U+2022) and `:` between single digits as separators in the mask too. Then add these cases to `OtpMaskTest` and `OtpFilterTest`.

findings.title: The mask joins digits across at most three spaces, but the filter reads any run of whitespace as one, so '482    913' with unlisted wording is stored readable
findings.detail: `OtpMask.MAX_SEPARATORS = 3`. `OtpFilter.sentences` collapses `\s+` to a single space before it looks for codes. So a code split by four or more spaces, or by spaces around a line break, is one code to the filter and two short numbers to the mask. When the wording has a strong keyword the filter drops it (`Your TAC is 482    913.` → `Drop(reason=OTP)`). With wording the lists don't hold (D119's whole reason for masking everything), it is kept unmasked: `Masukkan 482    913 untuk sahkan.` is stored exactly as posted. D119 says the mask reads digits "as the filter reads them … across spaces". Suggested fix: count any run of whitespace as one separator, as the filter does.

findings.title: 'A notification the filter can't read is kept masked and marked' has no test with teeth: making that branch unmark leaves every app test green
findings.detail: `CaptureGate.decide` sets `unread = true` when the filter throws. That covers `StackOverflowError` on the JVM and, since a6a2437, `RuntimeException`, Android's ICU regex failure. The flag ORs into `maybeOtp`. Changing either branch to `false`, or no longer catching `RuntimeException`, leaves all 41 core tests green (probes P8a, P8, P7b). `OtpMaskTest`'s long inputs assert no code is left, never the mark. The emulator test `a_very_long_notification_is_read_without_crashing_the_listener` asserts `maybeOtp`, but its text begins `Never share your TAC.`, so the mark comes from the OTP word whether or not the catch ran. That is how bc2219f shipped with the emulator dropping the 5,000-character notification as *unread*, which only a6a2437 caught. QA's `Probe6.ac25_unreadable_kept_masked_and_marked` uses a long sentence with **no** OTP word. It goes red when the overflow branch returns false. Suggested: add that case to `CaptureGateTest`. Make the emulator test's text word-free too ("Paid RM12.90 at KEDAI MAJU. " + digits), so it proves the catch on ART.

findings.title: Captured on this phone still says 'as the apps wrote them', and patterns.md §7 still says 'exactly as the app wrote them', but under D119 every row may carry masked numbers with no line to explain them
findings.detail: Since D119, every kept notification has its 4+ digit runs masked, marked or not. Ryt's *Your money is in!* now reads `… on ••/•/••••, 9:48 PM (GMT+8).`, and a Grab charge reads `for booking •••••••••••-K4XQ2PLM7RTWA-G-1`. The muted line appears only under a *maybe OTP* row, as D119 says. The screen's intro still promises `N notifications, newest first, as the apps wrote them.`, and `docs/ui/patterns.md` §7 (*Raw notification row*) still says "the title and the text exactly as the app wrote them". During the soak the owner reads this screen and shares from it, and will see bullets in Ryt dates under a claim that the text is verbatim. That is pattern drift: the screen and the pattern doc disagree with the spec. Suggested: intro copy such as *as the apps wrote them, with long numbers hidden*, and a D119 line in patterns.md §7.

findings.title: The simulator still can't post arbitrary text, and its dedupe identity isn't the shell's
findings.detail: Run 5's note 6 still stands. The dev panel posts four fixed samples, a fixed OTP and a fixed, already-masked maybe-OTP, so a browser walk proves the screen, never the mask. The fixed samples do match the core: `Probe6.after_sim_sample_parity` checks Ryt's masked date, and `Probe5.ac59s` checks the maybe-OTP. The simulator also dedupes on `package, title, text, bigText, when` joined by NUL. It omits the notification key and isn't length-prefixed, so it isn't §6.2's key. That's harmless today, but a future flow that relies on the key in the browser would be misled. A dev-panel text field that posts through a TypeScript copy of the gate is out of scope for B02; recorded for B07/B09.
findings.evidence: const key = (e) => [e.package, e.title, e.text, e.bigText, e.when].join('\u0000');

findings.title: A notification with no `when` is stored with its post time as `when`, so the outbox can't tell 'none' from a real stamp
findings.detail: `CaptureGate`: `val whenMillis = if (p.whenMillis > 0) p.whenMillis else p.postTime`. That value goes into both the dedupe key and `when_ms`. §6.2 lists the post time and `when` ("the time the app stamped on it") as separate raw fields. A replay of a notification with no `when` still dedupes, because Android keeps `postTime` across a replay. But the soak question about how each app updates a notification (§6.2: "an update may get a new `when`") can't be answered for apps that stamp none. Worth a line in D115 or the handoff, or storing 0 in `when_ms` and using the fallback only for the key. B07 derives ids from the key, so decide before events sync.
findings.repro: CaptureGateTest `no when falls back to the post time`

See finding 12 for the missing unit test.
